flags.title: Legs feel ready before they are

answers.question: I feel ready. Can I go back to 40 miles next week and start speedwork for the 10K?
answers.answer:
Not yet on either, but you're close. Plan on about 21 easy miles this week with strides, then build to the mid-30s over three weeks. Jumping from 12 to 40 miles a week after a marathon would more than triple your miles while your quads are still rebuilding.

If you race the Thanksgiving 10K on Thu Nov 26, faster running comes back in steps:

| Week | Miles | Faster running |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oct 26 – Nov 1 | about 21 | strides only |
| Nov 2 – 8 | about 28 | first light session, such as a fartlek |
| Nov 9 – 15 | about 33 | a session at 10K pace |
| Nov 16 – 22 | about 35 | a sharper 10K session |
| Nov 23 – 29 | about 15, including the race | a short tune-up early in the week, race Thursday |

Four weeks is enough to sharpen up for a good 10K, though you won't be at your peak. In your next check-in, tell me whether you're committing to the 10K. Also tell me what comes after, such as a spring marathon to chase 3:45, so I can plan for both.

new.analysis:
## Last week
You followed the plan exactly. You ran all three easy runs at their planned distances, took all four rest days and added nothing. That restraint is a big part of why you feel this good a week after a marathon.

Your runs back up what you said in your check-in. How good you felt went from 5 to 7 to 8 out of 10 across the three runs, and pain stayed at 0. Sunday's 9:51/mi at heart rate 139 almost exactly matches your easy runs before the race, so you haven't lost aerobic fitness.

The only thing you missed was strength. You planned one session and did none, so it's back on Thursday after a short run. It matters more now than during the build, because the race showed exactly where you broke down.

## This week
The plan brings back runs first, then distance, then speed. This week goes from three to five runs of 3 to 6 miles, about 21 miles in total, which is roughly half your biggest weeks. Strides are the only faster running, and flat routes save your quads from downhill pounding while they finish rebuilding.

## The race
The race was 12 minutes faster than your first marathon, and it taught a clear lesson. You held about 8:30/mi, right on 3:45 pace, until around mile 21. Then your quads gave out and you slowed to about 9:30/mi.

When the race moved two weeks earlier, you lost time for a second 20-miler. Your legs gave out before your fitness did. That points to durability as the gap, not speed.

If you chase 3:45 again, the work is durability. More long runs of 18 to 22 miles, some finishing at marathon pace, plus regular strength work would target the miles where the race fell apart. Your marathon-pace sessions at 8:30 to 8:35/mi already showed you have the speed.
